correctness.rationale: For N>=5 the two adjacent cosine samples around the angle 3π/4 have opposite signs for cos(2θ). A positive linear combination of the two active nonnegativity inequalities eliminates the free second-harmonic coefficient and yields the stated upper bound. The proposed extremizer factors as a positive constant times (x-u)(x-v), which is nonnegative on every grid sample because u and v are adjacent in the monotone cosine list. The 8|N boundary is handled separately by the zero second-harmonic coefficient at the critical sample. The comparison with sqrt(2) factors exactly, proving the equality criterion and limit. The standalone numerical verifier independently checks finite cases but is not used to infer the infinite theorem.

originality.rationale: The all-modulus statement was compared at statement level with the exact discrete Carathéodory–Fejér formulation, the equivalent second discrete Fejér problem, and later selected-case theorems. Ivanov–Ivanov (2010) explicitly say their second discrete problem was then solved only for the highest coefficient; the target (ν,p)=(1,3) is outside that family. Ivanov (2018) later covers N=6,7,9 in equivalent notation, and those values agree with the new formula, but the inspected theorems do not give λ(1,3,N) for arbitrary N. The 2003 broader-support interval formula and general LCA reductions likewise do not imply the fixed singleton result.
residual_risks: A differently indexed discrete extremal-polynomial paper may contain the same all-modulus degree-two formula.
Finite-dimensional sampled-positivity results may encode the adjacent-root formula without Carathéodory–Fejér or Turán terminology.

value.rationale: The fixed degree-two problem is the first nontrivial discretized Carathéodory–Fejér case with a genuinely free higher harmonic. The theorem gives an exact answer for every cyclic grid, identifies precisely when sampling changes the classical Fejér constant, and supplies an explicit extremizer. This is a natural structural refinement of a named extremal problem rather than an arbitrary finite computation.
